title: Poems in the dark
hookLine: in prison he composes his great love poem in his head

lines: NO PHONE, NO BOOKS, NO PAPER.
cards: Lock a person in a closet for months, no phone, no books, no paper, and what does the mind do? It could replay every wrong ever done to it. It could plan revenge, or despair, or both.
John of the Cross, cold and sick in his cell in Toledo, did something else. He started making poems. Not angry poems.
Love poems. With nothing to write with, he composed them in his head, line by line, and kept them there, memorized, in the dark. Poems still read today began that way.

teach.h: A LOVE SONG FOR THE SOUL.
teach.b: First, the Canticle. One poem he began there is known as the Spiritual Canticle, a love song modeled on the Song of Songs in the Bible. A bride searches everywhere for her beloved, who has slipped away.
For John, the bride is the soul and the beloved is God. He made the first part of it in that cell, keeping the stanzas in memory.

teach.h: A KIND JAILER, A LITTLE PAPER.
teach.b: Second, the kind jailer. After some months, the story goes, a new, younger friar was put in charge of him. He was gentler, let John out to empty his bucket, and gave him a pen and a little paper.

That's how some of the poems survived. Third, the spring. One of the poems from the cell has a refrain that keeps coming back, in John's Spanish: "Que bien sé yo la fonte que mana y corre, aunque es de noche."

teach.h: I KNOW THE SPRING, THOUGH IT IS NIGHT.
teach.b: How well I know the spring that rushes and flows, although it is night. Remember where he made it. No light.

teach.h: WHAT YOU KNOW BY HEART STAYS.
teach.b: And he says: I know where the water is. Even at night. Fourth, the psalms.
For years he had prayed the psalms day after day, in the Church's daily prayer.
When everything else was taken away, what was in his memory was still his: the Bible's love poetry and the psalms' cries were the raw material.
In the Douay-Rheims: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me." What you've memorized can't be confiscated.

how: Carmelites and many other Catholics read and pray John's poems, especially the Spiritual Canticle, and memorizing psalms and short scripture verses remains a common Catholic devotional habit.

games.q: you're locked in a dark closet for months with nothing to read or write with. what do you do with your mind?
o: replay every wrong done to you.
compose love poems in your head and memorize them.
sleep as much as you can.
games.why: John made love poems to God, still read today, and kept them in memory until he had paper.

practice: Take one line of a psalm: though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. Say it once slowly, again with your eyes closed, then once more only in your head.
If you pray, let it be a prayer; if you don't, let it be something to carry that no one can take.
